newsitem.title: ROMANIA: S.Korea's Daewoo sees Romania steep car sales drop.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Daewoo sees Romania steep car sales drop.

text.p: South Korea's Daewoo Heavy Industries Ltd car venture in Romania has laid off thousands of employees and suspended production for a week after a sharp drop in sales, the company said on Wednesday.

"We are stuck with a yard full of cars and had to stop production and send most of our staff off on enforced holidays," Andrei Radu, spokesman for Rodae Automobile told Reuters from Craiova, 300 km (180 miles) west of the capital.

Radu said the measure to halt production was mainly due to poor sales in the past three months following price increases and deep cuts in Romanians' purchasing power. Employees will return to work next Monday but are to have a further 10-day enforced holiday at Orthodox Easter at the end of the month.
He gave no details of the number of temporary layoffs but said only a small number of sales and maintenance people on the staff of 5,000 remained at work.

Daily production at the plant had been reduced in the past two months to 75 cars from 165 at the end of last year and monthly sales fell to 200 cars from 3,000 over the same period. Stocks stand at 15,000 vehicles.
The plant opened last year and produced 23,000 cars and plans had called for production of 75,000 units this year.

Radu said the company planned now to export models to its plants in Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Russia. "The first 144 cars left on Tuesday for our plant in Lublin (Poland) and from May we will export 3,000 cars per month," he said.
Rodae Automobile, which produces the Cielo model, is a joint venture of Daewoo Heavy Industries and Automobile Craiova local car maker, with the Koreans holding a 51 percent stake.
Cielos are exported to Poland disassembled to avoid heavy customs duties. The model sells for up to $13,600 in Romania.

Daewoo Heavy Industries is the largest single investor in Romania with $210 million pumped in the Craiova plant since 1994 and plans to inject $1.0 billion by the year 2000. -- Diana Voicu, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
